snippet.title: Bank of America's CEO, Asked How Many Borrowers Lost Their Homes: "Probably Around a Million"
snippet.description:
Rep. Madeleine Dean questions Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan about foreclosures at the House Financial Services Committee's "Holding Megabanks Accountable" hearing on April 10, 2019. Earlier, Dean described a family member's struggle to get a mortgage modification from the bank, and Moynihan said: "We did a lot of them. And so I apologize if your constituent at the time wasn't treated right." Dean: "You have lawsuits against you for this same practice? Over and over again. It was not just one person." Moynihan: "We had a settlement, like all of us did. We did everything in that settlement. An independent monitor looked at it and said we were in full compliance." Dean: "How many people lost their homes?" Moynihan: "The precise number of people who lost their homes in America was around--" Dean: "Your borrowers. How many of your borrowers lost their homes?" Moynihan: "Total foreclosures done since 2006 when housing costs quit going up on pieces of property were probably around a million." Dean: "A million of your customers lost their homes." Moynihan: "And 2 million were modified." Dean: "Did you ever take the time to meet with some of those folks who lost their homes?" Moynihan: "I received e-mails from them. I assured, when I met with Senator Reed and he asked us if we could open up centers, we opened up 26 centers." He added that the bank put on 50,000 people, and that the HAMP incentive money it received was nothing compared to what modifications cost.

In February 2012 federal and state officials announced a $25 billion mortgage servicing settlement with the five largest servicers. Bank of America's share was about $11.8 billion, including about $7.6 billion of borrower assistance, according to its SEC filing. The figure of about a million foreclosures is Moynihan's own estimate from this hearing.

Sources: U.S. House Committee on Financial Services, "Holding Megabanks Accountable: A Review of Global Systemically Important Banks 10 Years After the Financial Crisis," April 10, 2019 (U.S. government work, public domain), youtube.com/watch?v=j68ZutW2gUA; hearing transcript (govinfo.gov, CHRG-116hhrg37449); Bank of America Form 8-K, February 9, 2012 (SEC filing); U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development press release, February 9, 2012 (National Mortgage Settlement).

snippet.title: Florida Stayed British on Independence Day… Then It Went to Spain, Not America 🗺️
snippet.description:
Independence Day, 1776: thirteen colonies declared independence, but Britain's two Florida colonies, East and West Florida, did not join them 🗺️ The Continental Congress had written to both; neither sent delegates. British West Florida stretched across parts of four of today's states (Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana), which is why a corner of Louisiana is still called the Florida Parishes. Britain only got Florida in 1763: it had captured Havana in 1762, and in the Treaty of Paris Spain gave up Florida to get Havana back (Article XX), while France ceded its coast east of the Mississippi, except New Orleans (Article VII). No Native nation living here signed that treaty. In 1764 Britain moved West Florida's northern border up from the 31st parallel. During the Revolution a crowd in St Augustine burned effigies of Samuel Adams and John Hancock, loyalists poured in from Georgia and the Carolinas (East Florida's colonial population is estimated at about 3,000 in 1776 and about 17,000 by 1783-84), and an American invasion of East Florida was defeated at Thomas Creek in 1777. After the British took Charleston in May 1780, three signers of the Declaration, Thomas Heyward Jr., Arthur Middleton and Edward Rutledge, were held as prisoners of war in St Augustine until July 1781. Meanwhile Spain, at war with Britain from 1779 as France's ally, took Baton Rouge, Mobile and, after two months of fighting, Pensacola (May 1781). On 3 September 1783 Britain signed two treaties: one recognised the independence of the United States, the other ceded East and West Florida to Spain (Article V; St Augustine was handed over in July 1784). The United States got Spain's remaining Florida in 1821 (Adams-Onís Treaty, signed 1819). Today, Pensacola calls itself the City of Five Flags.
